thread.title: Curtis calls for stable regulations during Senate review of toxic substance law
thread.title_full: Curtis calls for stable regulations during Senate review of toxic substance law

author: beehive state news
title: Curtis calls for stable regulations during Senate review of toxic substance law
text:
During a U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee hearing on the reauthorization of the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA), Senator John Curtis (R-Utah) called for a more predictable regulatory system for chemicals that balances public health protection with the need for American industry to innovate and compete globally.
Senator Curtis stated, “I have been looking forward to this hearing to examine the regulatory environment for new and existing chemicals and its impact on innovation, safety, and American competitiveness.
“American companies invest billions of dollars each year in research and development to create materials that reduce emissions, improve safety, and strengthen our industrial base. But when reviews under TSCA are delayed, unpredictable, or disconnected from real-world applications, innovation slows. Research moves overseas. Promising replacements are shelved. American workers lose opportunities.
“There are few industries impacted more than semiconductors, which are critical to American and allied competitiveness. Advanced chips depend on highly specialized chemicals that are essential to nearly every aspect of modern life.
“My wife and I spent several years living and working in Taiwan, and I saw firsthand how a strategic investment in semiconductors transformed its economy from producing Christmas lights to becoming a global semiconductor powerhouse that now invests in advanced facilities here in the United States.
“One anecdote that stayed with me from our Subcommittee hearing in October is that, in some cases, aircraft are required to use an environmentally inferior chemical in the cargo hold even though a safer alternative has been approved for use in the passenger cabin of the same aircraft. That restriction stems not from aviation safety regulators, but from EPA’s TSCA program.
“Even small formulation changes can trigger new reviews, delaying safer or more sustainable alternatives and disrupting entire supply chains.
“As we consider TSCA reauthorization, we should ensure the law allows manufacturers to build world-class products that meet the highest safety standards, while also providing certainty to companies that they can access the chemicals necessary to meet specifications or requirements.
“The question is not whether to regulate chemicals. Most recognize the value and importance of TSCA. The question is how we make domestic chemical manufacturing both predictable and safe.”
Curtis questioned whether it was necessary for EPA to issue Significant New Use Rules (SNURs) for every new chemical: “When EPA evaluates Pre-Manufacture Notices, is it necessary to issue a Significant New Use Rule for every new chemical? It seems we’re effectively permitting an innovation and immediately regulating it in a way Congress did not intend. Also, when EPA does determine that a SNUR is appropriate, is there a more effective way to issue it so companies can bring their products to the market without unnecessary delays?”
Dr. Richard Engler of the Coalition for Chemical Innovation responded: “EPA has been issuing SNURs or some restriction on 85-90% of new chemicals. It’s not every new chemical. Again, if EPA finds it is low [risk], EPA will let it go forward without a restriction. But many of the products that we’ve assisted clients bringing through the new chemicals program…we’ve demonstrated to EPA—mathematically—that it is extraordinarily unlikely that any release or exposure would exceed EPA’s concern threshold. Yet, EPA proceeds with the restriction…So I think no; it’s not necessary for EPA to take that level of restriction…but that’s what we’ve been seeing now across four different administrations.”
Discussing ways to improve review predictability under TSCA through stewardship pathways rather than broad inventory listings, Curtis asked Dr. Michal Freedhoff if such an approach could help streamline assessments: “Does this structure provide EPA assessors with a stronger basis to evaluate a chemical based on its intended use…Would that improve predictability in the review process?”
Freedhoff replied: “I appreciate the creativity of this idea…and I agree that by not listing…the stewardship chemicals on the inventory…it ensures that EPA would have to review them later if someone else wanted…to use [them] for a different purpose…but I still think…this pathway would be quite difficult for EPA…to implement…and would probably divert staff away from reviewing new chemicals while they figured out how…to implement…the program.”
Curtis concluded: “Could we agree that it’s a good conversation to have?” To which Freedhoff answered: “I think it’s great…to think of ways…that EPA could protect people while meeting its deadlines.” Curtis added: “Thank you…I would love…to further that conversation with you.”
Addressing challenges faced by semiconductor manufacturers due to regulatory transitions as China expands its capabilities in this sector, Curtis asked David Isaacs of Semiconductor Industry Association about lessons learned regarding consistency within regulatory frameworks:
Isaacs responded: “Yes; this is one factor very much…in driving new investment…Our industry is very competitive…and United States is in global race…Having more certainty…and predictability with regard…to being able introduce new substances…is very important…That’s why we think there should be targeted reforms…streamline process…[not] open-ended exemptions…[but] reviews based on conditions-of-use…”
Curtis emphasized: “I’d like highlight words you use—they’re consistency and predictability—it’s not shortcuts…it’s just like what is drill?…Let’s not change it…and let’s be predictable…and consistent.”
